title: Recent Inflation Developments and Challenges for Research and Monetary Policymaking
summary: Former Cleveland Fed President Loretta Mester delivered this speech at the Konstanz Seminar in May 2016, discussing why inflation had remained persistently below central bank targets in the US, UK, and Euro area following the Great Recession. She reviewed factors suppressing inflation including weak global demand, declining commodity prices, and US dollar appreciation, and discussed the empirical relationship between dollar strength and inflation suppression. Mester emphasized the importance of continued research into inflation dynamics given the uncertainty they pose for monetary policymakers.
key_points: The Fed established its explicit 2% PCE inflation target in January 2012, which the FOMC views as symmetric (concerned when persistently above OR below target)
In 2015, inflation measured well below targets: US at 0.66% PCE, UK at 0.20% CPI, and Euro area at 0.25% HICP
Global demand was weak in the aftermath of the financial crisis and during the slow recovery from the Great Recession
Energy and commodity price declines, along with US dollar appreciation, have kept inflation suppressed
According to Fed SIGMA model simulations, a 10% rise in the real value of the dollar reduces core inflation by about 0.5% one year after the shock, partially reversing thereafter
These are Mester's personal views, not necessarily those of the FOMC or Federal Reserve System
why_it_matters: While this speech is now 10 years old, it provides historical context for understanding the persistent below-target inflation that characterized the post-Great Recession era across major economies. The speech notes that inflation running below target is as concerning to the FOMC as inflation above target, a symmetric framework that remains relevant.
macro_context: The speech contextualizes low inflation as a global phenomenon driven by three primary forces: (1) weak global demand in the aftermath of the financial crisis, (2) declining energy and commodity prices, and (3) US dollar appreciation putting downward pressure on import prices. The SIGMA model provides quantitative estimates of the dollar-inflation transmission mechanism.
important_numbers: 0.5% — estimated decline in core inflation one year after a 10% dollar appreciation shock
